title: Conduct a financial analysis of a small business

lessons.title: Financial statements of a small business
lessons.html:
Why analyse the finances?

A small business can be busy every day and still be losing money. Financial analysis tells the owner whether the business is profitable, whether it can pay its bills, and where to improve. It is based on three main financial statements.

1. Income statement (profit and loss)

Shows income and expenses over a period, such as a year or a season.

ItemExample (R)
Sales600 000
Less cost of sales360 000
Gross profit240 000
Less operating expenses (wages, electricity, fuel, rent)180 000
Net profit before tax60 000

2. Balance sheet (statement of financial position)

Shows what the business owns and owes on a specific date.

  • Assets: what it owns. Current assets include cash, stock and money owed by customers (debtors). Non-current assets include vehicles, cold rooms and equipment.
  • Liabilities: what it owes. Current liabilities include creditors and short-term loans. Long-term liabilities include a bank loan over five years.
  • Owner's equity: assets minus liabilities.

3. Cash flow statement

Shows actual cash coming in and going out. Profit and cash are not the same: a packhouse may show a profit but have no cash because the exporter has not yet paid for the fruit. Many small businesses fail because they run out of cash, not because they are unprofitable.

Good records come first

The statements are only as good as the records behind them. Keep invoices, receipts, bank statements, wage records and stock counts, and record transactions regularly in a cash book or accounting software.

lessons.title: Ratios, interpretation and action
lessons.html:
Key ratios

Ratios make numbers easier to compare from year to year or with similar businesses. Using the example income statement (sales R600 000, gross profit R240 000, net profit R60 000):

  • Gross profit margin = gross profit divided by sales x 100 = 240 000 / 600 000 x 100 = 40 percent.
  • Net profit margin = net profit divided by sales x 100 = 60 000 / 600 000 x 100 = 10 percent.

Liquidity ratios show whether the business can pay short-term debts:

  • Current ratio = current assets divided by current liabilities. If current assets are R150 000 and current liabilities R100 000, the ratio is 1.5. A ratio below 1 means the business may not be able to pay its short-term debts.
  • Acid test (quick) ratio = (current assets minus stock) divided by current liabilities. It excludes stock because stock may not sell quickly.

Solvency and return:

  • Debt ratio = total liabilities divided by total assets. A high ratio means the business relies heavily on borrowed money.
  • Return on investment = net profit divided by owner's equity x 100. It shows what the owner earns on the money invested.

Interpreting the results

Do not look at one number alone. Compare:

  • this year with last year (trend);
  • actual results with the budget;
  • your business with industry norms where available.

Example: gross margin fell from 45 to 40 percent. Investigation shows packaging prices rose but selling prices stayed the same. The owner can negotiate with suppliers, change packaging or raise prices.

Taking action

  • Cut unnecessary expenses and control waste.
  • Improve cash flow by invoicing promptly and following up on debtors.
  • Negotiate payment terms with suppliers.
  • Review prices against costs regularly.
  • Consult an accountant for tax and complex decisions.

Key points

  • The income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement are the basis of analysis.
  • Profit is not the same as cash.
  • Gross and net profit margins measure profitability.
  • The current and acid test ratios measure liquidity.
  • Compare ratios over time and against budget, then act on what you find.
